To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) DTI abnormalities are not limited to the corticospinal tract but also involve gray structures of the fronto-subcortical circuit, (ii) DTI abnormalities in gray structures are associated with neuropsychological dysfuntions and (iii) DTI abnormalities may be used to identify ALS patients at risk for cognitive impairment.

we investigated whether microstructural abnormalities occurred in gray structures of frontal–sub-cortical circuits in ALS patients using diffusion tensor MRI (DTI) in a large cohort of 24 ALS subjects and 22 healthy control subjects.

we found that ALS patients have increased mean diffusivity values in several cortical structures, the caudate nucleus, the putamen, the globus pallidum, the thalamus, the amygdala and the hippocampus, and that the increased mean diffusivities correlate with the degree of neuropsychological impairment.

the development of a new method for the analysis and interpretation of diffusion tensor imaging data.

the frontal cortex and the subcortical structures that are part of the frontal-sub-cortical circuits are not spared by the degeneration in ALS.
ALS is not just a motor disease, but a multisystem disorder with prominent frontal-subcortico-cerebellar involvement.
the ALS is not a pure motor disease and that it should be regarded as a multisystemic disorder with motor, cognitive and behavioral symptoms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ALS patients show a significant increase of MD values in the frontal cortex and subcortically in caudate, thalamus and hippocampus compared to controls.
the DTI changes in gray structures in ALS are consistent with the multisystemic degenerative process in ALS, and that these changes are correlated with the neuropsychological impairment.
the gray structures of the circuits are involved in the pathophysiology of ALS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DTI is a useful tool to investigate the microstructural changes in ALS.

DTI can be used to investigate gray matter structures and their involvement in the pathophysiology of ALS, which is a major step forward in understanding the disease and in the design of future therapies.
